All Are Welcome
awl ar WEL-kum
slogan (clause)
A churchly welcome-statement, true in its proper sense (the gospel call goes to all) but increasingly used as a banner of affirmation — 'all are welcome' as code for 'all relationships, identities, and lifestyles are blessed here, with no call to change.' The phrase echoes a common worship song refrain.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
A true gospel welcome until it drops the call to repent — the open door that leads nowhere, the table without the cross.

📖 Biblical Definition

The gospel invitation truly is universal in its offer: 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matt. 11:28); 'whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely' (Rev. 22:17); 'him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out' (John 6:37). The door is genuinely open to every sinner without exception of race, rank, or past. But the same Lord who welcomes all welcomes them to repentance: His first preaching was 'Repent ye, and believe the gospel' (Mark 1:15), and His parting word to the woman He did not condemn was 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11). The feast is for all who will come, but they come 'having a wedding garment' (Matt. 22:11-12) — the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith, not the rags of a life left unchanged. Welcome and repentance are not rivals; the welcome is a welcome to be made new.

📜 Origin & Era

A true gospel invitation (Matt. 11:28) weaponized to mean 'come as you are and stay as you are' — welcome without repentance, the table without the cross.

ALL ARE WELCOME, slogan. A church welcome-statement; true as the universal gospel offer, corrupted as a banner of unconditional affirmation.

True sense: the gospel call goes to every sinner without exception (Matt. 11:28; Rev. 22:17; John 6:37).

Corrupt sense: 'come as you are and stay as you are' — affirmation of every identity and lifestyle with no call to repent.

Rebutted by the terms of the welcome itself: 'Repent ye, and believe' (Mark 1:15); 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11); the required wedding garment (Matt. 22:11-12).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

John 6:37 — "All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."

Mark 1:15 — "And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel."

Matthew 22:11-12 — "And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless."

John 8:11 — "She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A true gospel invitation is bent to mean 'come as you are AND stay as you are' — welcome without repentance, the open door with no threshold, the table without the cross.

expand to see more

The corruption keeps the first half of the gospel and amputates the second. 'All are welcome' is gloriously true as the offer of Christ to sinners: the door is open to the adulterer, the proud, the addict, the self-righteous, every kind of fallen man. But the welcome is a welcome to a Person who saves from sin, not a ratification of sin. The corrupted slogan severs the call from its object: it keeps 'come as you are' and quietly drops 'and be made new,' so that the church's open door no longer leads anywhere — not to repentance, not to the cross, not to a changed life, only to an endless affirmation of the sinner exactly as the sin left him. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the slogan's affirming sense is named here to rebut it.

Christ shows the right shape. He welcomed the woman taken in adultery without a stone — 'neither do I condemn thee' — and in the same breath sent her out changed: 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11). The two halves are inseparable; to keep the first without the second is not mercy but cruelty, leaving a soul comfortable in what condemns it. The wedding parable presses the point: the king's invitation truly goes out to all in the highways (Matt. 22:9-10), yet the guest without the wedding garment — without Christ's righteousness put on by faith — is cast out (22:11-13). All are welcome to come; none is welcome to remain unclothed.

The recovery is to preach both the open door and the narrow gate. The gospel is the most welcoming word ever spoken — 'whosoever will' (Rev. 22:17) — and the most demanding, for the welcome is to take up a cross and follow (Luke 9:23). A church that says 'all are welcome' and means 'no one need change' has not out-loved Christ; it has betrayed the very souls it flatters. True welcome says: come, exactly as you are, with nothing in your hands — and be washed, justified, sanctified, made new (1 Cor. 6:11).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The universal gospel offer (Matt. 11:28) bent into unconditional affirmation; Christ welcomes all to repentance — 'go, and sin no more' — not to remain unchanged. Welcome and the cross are inseparable.

expand to see more

English: a church welcome-statement, true as the gospel offer, corrupted into a banner of affirmation.

Gospel offer: 'whosoever will' (Rev. 22:17); 'him that cometh I will in no wise cast out' (John 6:37) — genuinely universal.

The threshold: 'Repent ye, and believe' (Mark 1:15) and the required wedding garment (Matt. 22:12) — welcome is to be made new, not to stay the same.

Usage

"'All are welcome' is the most welcoming word ever spoken — and it welcomes you to repentance, not to your sin made comfortable."

"Christ said 'neither do I condemn thee' and 'go, and sin no more' in one breath; keep both, or you have kept neither."

"The door is open to every sinner; none may stay at the feast without the wedding garment of Christ's righteousness."
